questions.question: Describe the characteristics of a river's upper course and the processes of erosion that operate there.
questions.expected_answer: Upper course: near source, steep gradient, narrow shallow rocky channel, fast flow and high energy in floods; mainly vertical erosion. Processes: hydraulic action, abrasion/corrasion (potholes), attrition, solution. Narrow, steep V-shaped valley with interlocking spurs; weathering and mass movement on valley sides. Many SA rivers drop over the Great Escarpment (e.g. Tugela over the Drakensberg).

questions.question: Explain, with the aid of the correct sequence, how a waterfall forms and retreats to form a gorge.
questions.expected_answer: Hard resistant rock over softer rock; differential erosion of soft rock creates a step; falling water erodes a plunge pool by hydraulic action and abrasion; spray/backsplash undercuts soft rock, leaving an overhang of hard rock; overhang collapses, blocks used for abrasion; repeated, so the waterfall retreats upstream (headward erosion), leaving a steep-sided gorge. Examples: Tugela (about 948 m, five drops), Howick (about 95 m), Augrabies (about 56 m, gorge about 18 km), Victoria Falls (about 108 m, zigzag gorges).

questions.question: Distinguish between rapids, gorges and canyons and explain the importance of these landforms to people.
questions.expected_answer: Rapids: steep, turbulent stretches over alternating hard/soft rock bands or boulders (rafting on the Orange). Gorge: narrow, steep-sided valley, often from waterfall retreat or rapid downcutting. Canyon: very large deep gorge, often in dry/uplifted plateaus with horizontal layers (Fish River Canyon about 160 km long, about 550 m deep; Blyde River Canyon; Grand Canyon). Importance: tourism and adventure sports, dam sites and hydroelectric power (Kariba, Lesotho Highlands), but barriers to navigation and transport, rockfall and flash flood hazards.
